mechanism: Incidence rate is the number of new cases divided by the total person-time contributed while participants are at risk and under observation.
vignette: A cohort contributes 2,500 person-years of disease-free observation. During follow-up, 50 participants develop the disease of interest.
distractors: 2 new cases per 1,000 person-years
5 new cases per 1,000 person-years
50 new cases per 1,000 person-years
200 new cases per 1,000 person-years
distractor_notes: 50 per 1,000 would imply 125 events over 2,500 person-years.
200 per 1,000 would imply 500 events over 2,500 person-years.
key_expl: Incidence rate = 50 / 2,500 person-years = 0.02 per person-year = 20 per 1,000 person-years.
objective: Calculate incidence rate using a person-time denominator.

sources.title: Principles of Epidemiology, Lesson 3 - Section 2
sources.support: CDC defines incidence rate/person-time rate as new cases divided by summed person-time at risk and provides worked examples.

sources.title: Principles of Epidemiology: Glossary
sources.support: CDC defines person-time rate and person-time denominators used in incidence-rate calculations.

mechanism: Secondary attack rate estimates transmission among susceptible contacts of primary cases and is calculated using new cases among contacts divided by the eligible contact population.
vignette: During a household outbreak, 8 primary cases occur in 8 different households. The households contain 40 people in total. During the next incubation period, 12 additional household contacts become ill.
lead: What is the secondary attack rate among household contacts?
distractor_notes: 20% results from dividing the 8 primary cases by the total household population and does not measure secondary spread.
30% results from 12/40 and incorrectly leaves the 8 primary cases in the contact denominator.
50% is not obtained from the eligible-contact denominator of 32.
60% does not follow the secondary attack-rate calculation.
key_expl: Eligible contacts = 40 − 8 primary cases = 32; secondary attack rate = 12/32 × 100 = 37.5%.
objective: Calculate a secondary attack rate by excluding primary cases from the contact denominator.
clues: 12 secondary cases in the next incubation period

sources.title: Principles of Epidemiology, Lesson 3 - Section 2
sources.support: CDC defines secondary attack rate as cases among contacts divided by contacts and gives an example subtracting primary cases from the household denominator.

sources.title: Principles of Epidemiology, Lesson 3 - Quiz Answers
sources.support: CDC demonstrates calculation of secondary attack rate using cases among contacts divided by the contact population.

mechanism: Case-fatality proportion is the proportion of incident cases of a particular disease who die from that disease and is a measure of disease severity.
vignette: An outbreak produces 240 confirmed cases of an infection. Six of these 240 patients die from complications directly attributable to the infection.
distractor_notes: 0.4% does not equal 6/240 × 100.
4% would correspond to roughly 10 deaths among 240 cases.
25% would require 60 deaths among 240 cases.
40% would require 96 deaths among 240 cases.
objective: Calculate case-fatality proportion and distinguish it from population mortality rates.

sources.title: Principles of Epidemiology, Lesson 3 - Section 3
sources.support: CDC defines case-fatality rate/proportion as cause-specific deaths among incident cases divided by total incident cases and identifies it as a measure of severity.

sources.title: Principles of Epidemiology, Lesson 3 - Section 1
sources.support: CDC classifies case-fatality rate as a proportion rather than a true person-time rate.

mechanism: Proportionate mortality is the fraction of all deaths in a population during a period that is attributable to a specified cause; its denominator is total deaths, not total population.
vignette: In one county during a year, 2,000 people die from all causes. Of these deaths, 500 are due to cardiovascular disease.
lead: What is the proportionate mortality due to cardiovascular disease?
distractor_notes: 2.5% would result from an incorrect denominator or decimal placement.
40% would correspond to 800 of 2,000 deaths.
75% would correspond to 1,500 of 2,000 deaths.
key_expl: Proportionate mortality = 500 cardiovascular deaths / 2,000 total deaths × 100 = 25%.
objective: Calculate proportionate mortality using all deaths as the denominator.

sources.title: Principles of Epidemiology, Lesson 3 - Section 3
sources.support: CDC defines proportionate mortality as deaths from a specified cause divided by deaths from all causes and emphasizes that it is not a population mortality rate.

sources.title: Principles of Epidemiology: Glossary
sources.support: CDC defines proportionate mortality as the proportion of all deaths attributable to a specified cause and explicitly states that the denominator is all deaths rather than the population.

mechanism: A cause-specific mortality rate uses deaths from one specified cause in the numerator and the mid-interval population in which those deaths occurred in the denominator.
vignette: A city with a midyear population of 500,000 records 100 deaths from lung cancer during the year.
lead: What is the cause-specific mortality rate from lung cancer per 100,000 population?
distractor_notes: 5 per 100,000 would correspond to 25 deaths in this population.
50 per 100,000 would correspond to 250 deaths.
200 per 100,000 would correspond to 1,000 deaths.
objective: Calculate a cause-specific mortality rate using a population denominator.

sources.title: Principles of Epidemiology, Lesson 3 - Section 3
sources.support: CDC defines cause-specific death rate as deaths assigned to a specific cause divided by the mid-interval population, commonly expressed per 100,000.

sources.title: Principles of Epidemiology: Glossary
sources.support: CDC defines epidemiologic rates as event frequency in a defined population over time and provides mortality-rate terminology.

system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
mechanism: Eliciting the patient's full list of concerns early and jointly prioritizing them reduces premature narrowing and helps address the issues that matter most within limited visit time.
vignette: At the start of a primary care visit, a patient says, “My back hurts, but I also need to ask about my blood pressure and a new skin spot.” The clinician has a 20-minute appointment.
lead: Which response is most appropriate initially?
correct: “Let's list everything you want to address today, then we'll decide together what to prioritize.”
distractors: Begin a detailed history of the back pain before clarifying whether there are any other concerns
Ask the patient to select a single concern and defer all others before reviewing the full agenda
Choose the blood-pressure concern as the priority without first discussing the patient's priorities
Defer the new skin spot to a future visit without first incorporating it into the visit agenda
distractor_notes: Starting detailed work on the first concern before establishing the full agenda risks premature narrowing when visit time is limited.
Forcing selection of one issue before collaborative agenda setting can leave important concerns undisclosed or unprioritized.
Unilateral clinician prioritization does not use the collaborative agenda-setting approach promoted by AHRQ.
Automatically deferring a stated concern before agenda setting bypasses collaborative prioritization.
key_expl: AHRQ recommends eliciting concerns and priorities and using agenda setting so patient and clinician can prioritize what can be addressed during the visit.
objective: Use collaborative agenda setting when a patient presents multiple concerns.
clues: multiple concerns stated at visit opening

sources.title: Be Prepared To Be Engaged
sources.support: AHRQ states that understanding patient concerns and priorities is key to a safe visit and promotes setting a visit agenda.

sources.title: Evidence-Based Strategies To Engage Patients and Families
sources.support: AHRQ identifies visit agenda setting as a strategy that improves communication, visit efficiency, and safety.

system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
mechanism: Routine validated alcohol screening delivered in a comfortable, patient-centered, nonjudgmental manner can reduce stigma, support more valid disclosure, and identify people who may need further assessment or intervention.
vignette: During an annual primary care visit, a 36-year-old patient becomes guarded when the clinician begins asking about alcohol use.
correct: Use a validated alcohol screen and ask in a neutral, nonjudgmental manner
distractors: Postpone screening until the patient independently volunteers concern about drinking
Ask only whether the patient considers their drinking a problem rather than using a validated screen
Begin by emphasizing the harms of alcohol before asking about the patient's pattern of use
Rely on a family member's estimate of alcohol use instead of screening the patient directly
distractor_notes: Routine screening is intended to identify risky alcohol use even when the patient has not independently raised a concern.
A single subjective self-label does not substitute for the validated screening approach recommended by NIAAA.
Leading with warnings is less patient-centered than the comfortable, nonjudgmental screening approach NIAAA recommends.
Family estimates do not replace direct validated patient screening as the initial routine approach.
key_expl: NIAAA recommends validated screening and comfortable, patient-centered, nonjudgmental conversations about alcohol; SAMHSA's SBIRT model uses screening as the first step in identifying risk and appropriate follow-up.
objective: Apply validated, patient-centered, nonjudgmental alcohol screening in routine care.

sources.title: Screen and Assess: Use Quick, Effective Methods
sources.support: NIAAA recommends validated screening/assessment and patient-centered, nonjudgmental conversations that reduce stigma and support accurate disclosure.

sources.title: SBIRT: Screening, Brief Intervention, and Referral to Treatment
sources.support: SAMHSA describes screening as the first step in identifying severity of substance use and matching brief intervention or treatment referral.

system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
diagnosis: Empathic acknowledgment and validation during conflict
mechanism: When a patient is angry or distressed, active listening plus explicit acknowledgment and validation of emotion helps maintain trust and opens space for problem solving; arguing or becoming defensive tends to escalate conflict.
vignette: A patient angrily says, “I've been waiting for hours and nobody here cares what happens to me!” There is no immediate safety threat.
lead: Which response is most appropriate first?
correct: “I can see how frustrated and ignored you're feeling. Tell me what has been most upsetting.”
distractors: “The delay is due to hospital workflow; let me first explain why it happened.”
“I assure you that the staff does care; now let's move on to your medical concerns.”
“What solution would you like us to provide for the wait?”
“I'll ask the charge nurse to discuss your complaint with you before we continue.”
distractor_notes: Leading with an explanation addresses facts before first acknowledging and validating the patient's emotion.
Reassurance and redirection can bypass the patient's expressed distress instead of first acknowledging and exploring it.
Immediate problem solving skips the AHRQ-supported first step of acknowledging and validating the emotion and understanding the concern.
Delegating the complaint before first acknowledging the patient's distress misses the immediate opportunity for empathic listening.
key_expl: AHRQ communication guidance emphasizes allowing expression of emotion, active listening, and acknowledging and validating feelings before moving to facts or next steps.
objective: Respond to an angry patient first with empathic acknowledgment, validation, and active listening when there is no safety threat.

sources.title: Disclosure Checklist
sources.support: AHRQ directs clinicians to actively listen and to allow, acknowledge, and validate patient emotions.

sources.title: Communication Assessment Guide
sources.support: AHRQ identifies empathy, active listening, patience, tact, and ability to withstand anger or criticism without taking it personally as effective communication competencies.

system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
mechanism: For uses and disclosures to which it applies, HIPAA requires reasonable efforts to limit PHI to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose; the rule has explicit exceptions, including disclosures between health care providers for treatment.
vignette: A hospital billing employee needs information to resolve a single insurance-payment discrepancy. The employee requests the patient's entire medical record even though only the procedure code, date, and charge are relevant.
lead: Which action best follows the HIPAA Privacy Rule?
correct: Limit the information used or disclosed to what is reasonably necessary for the payment purpose
distractors: Release the entire medical record because the request is related to payment
Refuse to use any protected health information for payment unless the patient gives a new written authorization
Apply the treatment-provider exception even though this request is for payment
Give all billing staff unrestricted access to the full record once a payment purpose is established
distractor_notes: Payment uses and disclosures remain subject to reasonable minimum-necessary limits; a payment purpose does not automatically justify the entire record.
HIPAA permits appropriate payment uses and disclosures without requiring a new authorization in this setting; the relevant issue is limiting PHI when minimum necessary applies.
The explicit minimum-necessary exception is for treatment disclosures or requests by health care providers, not this payment-purpose request.
HHS requires role-based access policies that limit workforce access to the PHI needed for job functions rather than unrestricted access.
key_expl: HHS states that covered entities must reasonably limit PHI used, disclosed, or requested for payment and health-care operations to the minimum necessary for the purpose.
objective: Apply HIPAA's minimum-necessary principle to a non-treatment payment use of PHI.
clues: entire chart requested when a few data elements suffice

sources.title: Minimum Necessary Requirement
sources.support: HHS explains that covered entities generally must take reasonable steps to limit PHI use/disclosure/request to the minimum necessary for the intended purpose and lists exceptions.

sources.title: Uses and Disclosures for Treatment, Payment, and Health Care Operations
sources.support: HHS states that minimum necessary applies to payment and health-care-operations disclosures/requests while provider-to-provider treatment disclosures are exempt.

system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
diagnosis: Best-interest standard when patient wishes are unknown
mechanism: When an incapacitated patient's specific prior wishes and values cannot be determined, surrogate decisions should be guided by the patient's best interests rather than the surrogate's personal preferences.
vignette: An unconscious patient lacks decision-making capacity and has no advance directive or prior statements about the current treatment choice. His legally authorized surrogate asks how to decide between two medically reasonable options.
lead: Which standard should guide the decision?
correct: Choose the option that best promotes the patient's interests, using known values or perspectives when available
distractors: Choose whichever option the surrogate personally would want for themself
Always choose the most technologically aggressive treatment
Use substituted judgment based on specific patient wishes that are not known
Let the clinician choose without involving the authorized surrogate
distractor_notes: The surrogate's own preferences are not the ethical decision standard for the patient.
Best interests does not automatically mean maximal intervention; burdens and likely benefits matter.
Substituted judgment depends on evidence of the patient's preferences or values; here those are unknown for this choice.
An authorized surrogate should participate in decision making rather than being bypassed without justification.
key_expl: VA ethics policy defines best interests as the standard when a patient's specific values and wishes are unknown, with the surrogate and health-care team considering optimal outcomes and known cultural, ethnic, or religious perspectives.
objective: Use the best-interest standard when an incapacitated patient's treatment preferences cannot be determined.
clues: no known prior wishes for the decision

sources.title: VHA Directive 1004.01(3): Informed Consent for Clinical Treatments and Procedures
sources.support: Current VHA policy states that when the patient's specific values and wishes are unknown, surrogate treatment decisions must use the patient's best interests.

sources.title: Patient Rights - Veterans Health Administration
sources.support: VA patient-rights guidance states that when a decision maker does not know what the Veteran would want, the treatment team can help consider the Veteran's best interest.

system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
diagnosis: Medication reconciliation at transitions of care
mechanism: Medication reconciliation obtains and verifies the patient's medication history, compares it with new orders at admission/transfer/discharge, identifies unintended discrepancies, and communicates an accurate updated list across transitions.
vignette: A patient is being discharged after hospitalization. His home medication list, inpatient orders, and proposed discharge prescriptions differ in several places, and the reasons for the differences are unclear.
lead: Which action is most appropriate before discharge?
correct: Compare the lists, clarify unintended discrepancies, document intentional changes, and communicate the updated regimen to the patient and next clinician
distractors: Copy the inpatient medication list directly into discharge instructions without comparison
Delete all preadmission medications because hospitalization automatically replaces them
Ask the patient to decide which conflicting doses are correct without verification
Wait until the next outpatient visit to reconcile the lists
distractor_notes: Medication reconciliation specifically requires comparison rather than blindly copying one list.
Preadmission medications may need continuation, modification, or discontinuation based on the care plan; they are not automatically deleted.
Patients are important sources, but discrepancies require clinical verification and reconciliation.
Deferring known discrepancies across a transition increases medication-error risk.
key_expl: AHRQ's MATCH process calls for comparing current/discharge orders with preadmission medications, clarifying unintended differences, counseling the patient, and communicating the final list to the next provider.
objective: Apply medication reconciliation to prevent unintended discrepancies during care transitions.

sources.title: MATCH Toolkit - Appendix: Medication Reconciliation
sources.support: AHRQ specifies obtaining and confirming a medication history, reconciling orders, resolving unintended discrepancies, and communicating the discharge list to the patient and next provider.

sources.title: MATCH Toolkit - Designing the Medication Reconciliation Process
sources.support: AHRQ recommends a single accurate medication list and states that medication reconciliation should be integral to handoffs and transitions of care.

system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
diagnosis: Emergency exception to express consent for an incapacitated patient
mechanism: In a medical emergency, necessary care may proceed without the patient's express consent when immediate care is needed to preserve life or prevent serious health impairment, the patient is unable to consent, and there is no surrogate or waiting for surrogate consent would increase the hazard to the patient's life or health.
vignette: At a VA emergency department, an unconscious trauma patient has life-threatening internal bleeding and requires immediate surgery. No surrogate is reachable, no advance directive or prior refusal is known, and delaying surgery to locate a surrogate would materially increase the risk of death.
correct: Proceed with necessary emergency treatment under the emergency exception to express consent
distractors: Provide temporary stabilization but delay the necessary surgery until a surrogate can be reached
Treat an unrelated hospital employee as the surrogate because that person is immediately available
Wait for a court order because the surgery would ordinarily require signature consent
Infer that the patient refuses surgery because no written consent can be obtained
distractor_notes: When delay to obtain surrogate consent would increase the hazard to life or health, VA policy and 38 CFR 17.32 allow necessary emergency care to proceed without express consent.
An unrelated employee does not become an authorized surrogate merely by being available; the emergency exception addresses the situation when no surrogate is available or waiting would be hazardous.
The emergency exception permits necessary care without express consent when its criteria are met; a court order is not a prerequisite in this scenario.
Inability to obtain written consent from an incapacitated patient does not establish refusal; previously stated wishes must be followed when they are known and applicable.
key_expl: Current VHA Directive 1004.01 and 38 CFR 17.32 permit necessary emergency care without express consent when immediate care is required to preserve life or prevent serious health impairment, the patient cannot consent, and no surrogate is available or waiting for surrogate consent would increase the hazard.
objective: Apply the emergency exception to express consent when an incapacitated patient requires immediate life-preserving treatment and surrogate delay would increase risk.
clues: no surrogate/prior refusal and dangerous delay

sources.title: VHA Directive 1004.01(3): Informed Consent for Clinical Treatments and Procedures
sources.support: Current VHA Directive 1004.01, section 5.a, permits necessary emergency care without express consent when immediate care is needed to preserve life or prevent serious impairment, the patient cannot consent, and no surrogate is available or waiting for surrogate consent would increase hazard.

sources.title: 38 CFR 17.32 - Informed consent and advance directives
sources.support: Current eCFR section 17.32(c)(7) codifies the emergency exception to express consent using the same three conditions: immediate care need, inability to consent, and no surrogate or hazardous delay in obtaining surrogate consent.
